what_it_does: Before deploying a neural network on a specific chip (say, a phone's processor), engineers must 'tune' the program that runs the network — choosing among thousands of possible ways to schedule the computations so the chip's specific hardware is used efficiently. This search is slow because the main evaluation tool is a learned cost model (a secondary neural network that predicts how long a schedule will take) which is accurate but expensive to run on every candidate. Pruner introduces a two-stage approach: first, a fast symbolic analyzer (which uses algebra rather than learned predictions) quickly scores all candidates and keeps only a small promising subset; second, the slow accurate cost model evaluates only that subset. A companion technique called MoA-Pruner additionally adapts the cost model in real time when moving to a new chip, using incremental gradient updates rather than full retraining, so the model stays accurate without starting from scratch.
